listeningParts.title: Volunteering at a music festival
listeningParts.contextDescription: A student phones a festival organiser to ask about volunteering.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Hello, Greenvale Music Festival volunteer office, Martha speaking.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Hi, I saw on your website that you're looking for volunteers for this summer's festival, and I'd like to find out more.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Great, thanks for calling. The festival runs for three days, from Friday the eighth of August to Sunday the tenth. Volunteers work three shifts of eight hours during the festival, and in return you get a free ticket for the whole weekend, which normally costs two hundred and forty pounds.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: That sounds like a good deal. What kind of jobs are there?

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: There are several teams. The biggest is the stewarding team, which helps with crowd safety, checking tickets at the gates and giving directions. Then there's the recycling team, which collects and sorts waste around the site. We're trying to reduce the amount that goes to landfill, so it's an important job. We also have volunteers in the information tents and at the children's area.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: I think I'd be most interested in the children's area. I've worked at a summer camp before.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: That's useful experience. For the children's area, you need to be at least twenty-one, and you'll need a background check, which we arrange for you free of charge. How old are you?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: I'm twenty-two.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Perfect. The children's area runs activities like face painting, craft workshops and storytelling, and there's a small stage for children's bands. Shifts there are during the day only, between ten in the morning and six in the evening, so you'd have your evenings free to see the main bands.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Even better. Where do volunteers stay?

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: There's a separate volunteers' campsite, which is quieter than the main one and has its own showers and a kitchen tent. You need to bring your own tent and sleeping bag. Meals are provided during your shifts, and you'll get a voucher for one hot meal a day from any food stall on site.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Do I have to attend any training?

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Yes, all volunteers must attend an induction. There's an online session that takes about an hour, which you need to complete by the end of June. Then there's a short briefing on site on the Thursday afternoon, when you arrive and collect your wristband.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: And is there a deposit or anything like that?

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: There is. We ask for a deposit of the full ticket price when you sign up, which is returned to you after the festival as long as you complete all three shifts. It's unfortunate, but in the past some people signed up just to get a free ticket and then didn't turn up for work.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: That's fair. How do I get to the site? I don't drive.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: There's a free shuttle bus for volunteers from Hadley train station on the Thursday, leaving every half hour from twelve o'clock. Just show your volunteer email to the driver.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Great. Can I apply now?

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Yes, I can start the form. What's your full name?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Jasmine Whitlock. That's W-H-I-T-L-O-C-K.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: And an email address?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: It's jaswhit22 at mailbox dot com. That's J-A-S-W-H-I-T, then the numbers two, two.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Lovely. And do you have any special skills that might be useful? First aid, for example, or other languages?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: I've got a first-aid certificate from my summer camp job, and I speak some Italian.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Both very useful. I'll make a note. You'll receive an email with the link to the online induction and the deposit payment within the next two days. If you have any questions in the meantime, there's a page of frequently asked questions on the website.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: One more thing. Can I choose who I work with? A friend of mine might apply too.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Yes, just put your friend's name in the comments box on the form, and we'll try to put you on the same shifts, although we can't always guarantee it.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Thanks so much, Martha. I'm really looking forward to it.

listeningParts.title: Joining a community choir
listeningParts.contextDescription: The director of a community choir talks to people attending an open evening.

dialogue.speaker: Director
dialogue.text: Good evening, everybody, and welcome to the Riverside Community Choir open evening. I'm Grace Holloway, the musical director. It's lovely to see so many new faces. I'll tell you a bit about the choir, and then we'll sing a couple of songs together, so you can see what it's like.

dialogue.speaker: Director
dialogue.text: The choir was started twelve years ago by a group of friends who wanted to sing together just for fun. There were eight of them at the first rehearsal, in someone's living room. Today we have over ninety members, aged from eighteen to eighty-seven, and we rehearse here in the church hall every Tuesday evening from half past seven to nine thirty.

dialogue.speaker: Director
dialogue.text: The first thing I always want to make clear is that you don't need any experience to join, and there's no audition. Many of our members had never sung in a group before, and some told me they'd been told at school that they couldn't sing. In my experience, almost everyone can learn to sing in tune with a bit of practice and confidence.

dialogue.speaker: Director
dialogue.text: You also don't need to read music. We teach most of our songs by ear, which means I sing each line and you copy it. For those who do read music, we provide sheet music as well. We also record practice tracks for each part, which you can download from our website and listen to at home, in the car or wherever you like. Most members find these really helpful.

dialogue.speaker: Director
dialogue.text: The choir is divided into four sections, according to the range of your voice: sopranos and altos, who are usually women, and tenors and basses, who are usually men, although that's not a rule. If you're not sure which section you belong in, don't worry. After the first couple of weeks, I'll listen to you individually and help you decide.

dialogue.speaker: Director
dialogue.text: As for what we sing, we have a very wide range. There's pop, gospel, folk songs from around the world and some classical pieces. This term we're learning a medley of songs from musicals, as well as a traditional South African song, which has some wonderful harmonies.

dialogue.speaker: Director
dialogue.text: We perform about four times a year. Our biggest event is the Christmas concert in December, which raises money for a local charity. Last year we raised over three thousand dollars for the children's hospital. In summer we also sing outdoors at the town's riverside festival, and we occasionally visit care homes to sing for the residents, which is always a very moving experience.

dialogue.speaker: Director
dialogue.text: I'm often asked whether singing in a choir is good for you, and the answer seems to be yes. Research has found that group singing can reduce stress and improve mood, and many of our members say the choir is the highlight of their week. It's also very sociable. After each rehearsal, quite a few of us go to the café across the road.

dialogue.speaker: Director
dialogue.text: I should also mention that we have a small choir committee, made up of six members, who organise our concerts, social events and the annual weekend trip. This year we're going to the coast in May, where we'll take part in a choir festival with groups from all over the region. It's a wonderful chance to hear other choirs and make new friends, and everyone is welcome to come, whether or not they sing in the concert.

dialogue.speaker: Director
dialogue.text: Now, the practical details. Membership costs sixty dollars per term, and there are three terms a year. If that's difficult for you financially, please speak to me in private, as we have a fund to help people who can't afford it. Your first two rehearsals are free, so you can try it before deciding.

dialogue.speaker: Director
dialogue.text: Finally, please fill in one of the yellow forms on the table by the door before you leave, so we can add you to the email list. Right, let's warm up. Everybody stand up, take a deep breath, and stretch your arms above your head.

listeningParts.title: A project on music and memory
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two psychology students, Ravi and Ellie, discuss a project on music and memory with their supervisor.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: So, Ravi, Ellie, tell me where you've got to with your project on music and memory.

dialogue.speaker: Ravi
dialogue.text: We've finished the experiment, and we've just started analysing the results. As you know, we wanted to find out whether listening to background music affects how well students remember information.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: Remind me of the design.

dialogue.speaker: Ellie
dialogue.text: We had sixty participants, all undergraduate students. Each of them read a short article about the history of the Silk Road and then answered twenty questions about it. They did this in one of three conditions: in silence, with instrumental classical music, or with pop music that had lyrics.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: And how did you allocate people to the conditions?

dialogue.speaker: Ravi
dialogue.text: Randomly, using a computer program, so that there were twenty people in each group.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: And did all the participants read the article for the same length of time?

dialogue.speaker: Ellie
dialogue.text: Yes, everyone had exactly ten minutes to read it, and then they did a short puzzle for five minutes before answering the questions, so that they couldn't simply repeat what they'd just read.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: Good thinking. What did you find?

dialogue.speaker: Ellie
dialogue.text: The silent group did best, with an average score of fifteen out of twenty. The classical music group was only slightly lower, at fourteen. But the pop music group scored much lower, with an average of just under eleven.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: That's quite a big difference. How do you explain it?

dialogue.speaker: Ravi
dialogue.text: We think it's mainly the lyrics. When you're reading, you're processing language, and if you're also hearing words in a song, the two compete for the same mental resources. Instrumental music doesn't have that problem, or at least not as much.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: That fits with previous research. Did anything surprise you?

dialogue.speaker: Ellie
dialogue.text: Yes. We also asked participants whether they usually study with music. Those who said they always listened to music while studying did slightly better in the pop music condition than those who never did, but they still did worse than in silence.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: So being used to it helps a little, but doesn't remove the effect. That's interesting. Students often believe music helps them concentrate. Did you ask about that?

dialogue.speaker: Ravi
dialogue.text: We did. Most people in the pop music group thought the music hadn't affected them at all, even though their scores were lower. So people may not be very good at judging how distracting music is.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: That's a really important point to include in your discussion. Now, what about the limitations?

dialogue.speaker: Ellie
dialogue.text: Well, the sample was quite small, and all the participants were students, so we can't generalise to other age groups. Also, the test was immediately after reading, so we don't know about long-term memory.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: Anything else?

dialogue.speaker: Ravi
dialogue.text: We chose the music ourselves. People might be less distracted by music they know and like. Next time it might be better to let participants choose their own music.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: Good. You might also mention the volume. Did you control that?

dialogue.speaker: Ellie
dialogue.text: Yes, everyone used the same headphones at the same volume.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: Excellent. In your literature review, you might also want to look at research on music and memory in people with dementia. There's evidence that people with dementia can often remember songs from their youth long after other memories have faded, and some care homes use music to help residents feel calmer and communicate.

dialogue.speaker: Ravi
dialogue.text: That's fascinating. Is that because musical memory is stored differently in the brain?

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: That's one theory. Some studies suggest that the areas of the brain involved in musical memory are among the last to be damaged by the disease. But it's a different question from yours, so just mention it briefly.

dialogue.speaker: Ellie
dialogue.text: Okay. When would you like the draft?

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: Send me the results section by next Wednesday, and we'll meet again the week after.

listeningParts.title: The history of recorded sound
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a media history course on the development of sound recording.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good afternoon. Today we're going to look at the history of recorded sound. It's easy to forget that for almost all of human history, music could only be heard when it was performed live. If you wanted to hear a symphony, you had to go to a concert hall, and once the performance was over, the sound was gone forever. Recording changed not only how we listen to music, but music itself.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The first device that could record sound was invented not by Thomas Edison, as many people believe, but by a French printer named Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville, in 1857. His machine, which he called the phonautograph, used a horn to collect sound and a thin brush, called a stylus, which traced the sound waves as lines on paper covered with soot. However, Scott never intended his recordings to be played back. He wanted to study sound visually. Remarkably, in 2008, researchers in the United States used computer technology to convert some of his tracings into sound, and they were able to hear a person singing a French folk song recorded in 1860.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The first machine that could both record and play back sound was Edison's phonograph, in 1877. It used a cylinder wrapped in tin foil. As someone spoke into a horn, a needle cut a groove in the foil, and when the cylinder was turned again, the needle followed the groove and reproduced the sound. The first words Edison recorded were the children's rhyme 'Mary had a little lamb'. Interestingly, Edison originally thought the phonograph would be used mainly in offices, for dictating letters, rather than for entertainment.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Tin foil wore out after only a few plays, so it was soon replaced by wax cylinders. But cylinders were difficult to copy in large numbers. The solution came from a German-born inventor working in the United States, Emile Berliner, who in 1887 patented the gramophone, which used flat discs instead of cylinders. Discs could be produced from a master copy by pressing, rather like a stamp, which meant that thousands of identical copies could be made cheaply. This is the origin of the record industry.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Early recordings were made acoustically, without electricity. Musicians had to crowd around a large horn, and loud instruments like trumpets were placed further away than quiet ones. Many instruments simply didn't record well, and recordings could last only around three or four minutes per side. This is one reason why popular songs, even today, tend to be about three minutes long. From the mid-1920s, microphones and electrical recording greatly improved quality, and singers could perform more quietly and intimately, which led to new styles of singing.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The next major development was magnetic tape, developed in Germany in the 1930s. Tape allowed recordings to be edited by cutting and joining pieces, and later to be recorded on several separate tracks, so that different instruments could be recorded at different times and then combined. This transformed the recording studio into a creative tool, and by the 1960s, bands like the Beatles were producing albums that would have been impossible to perform live.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Meanwhile, records themselves improved. In 1948, the long-playing record, or LP, was introduced, which could hold over twenty minutes of music per side and was made of vinyl, which produced less noise than earlier materials. This made it possible to release albums rather than just single songs.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Then came the digital age. The compact disc, launched in 1982, stored sound as a series of numbers that were read by a laser. In the 1990s, the MP3 format compressed digital files by removing sounds that the human ear is less likely to notice, making it possible to share music over the internet. Today, most people listen through streaming services, which offer millions of songs instantly. Yet interestingly, sales of vinyl records have grown every year for well over a decade, as some listeners seek a more physical and deliberate experience. Next week, we'll look at how streaming has changed the economics of the music industry.

readingPassages.title: The invention of the piano
paragraphs: The piano is one of the most popular musical instruments in the world, found in concert halls, schools, churches and millions of homes. Yet compared with instruments such as the flute, the harp or the violin, it is a relatively recent invention. Its story is one of gradual technical improvement, driven by the demands of composers and performers and by changes in society.

Before the piano, the most important keyboard instruments were the harpsichord and the clavichord. In a harpsichord, pressing a key causes a small piece of quill or leather to pluck a string. This produces a bright, clear sound, but it has a significant limitation: however hard or softly the player presses the key, the volume stays almost the same. The clavichord, in which the strings are struck by small metal blades, could vary its volume, but its sound was so quiet that it was suitable only for small rooms.

The solution was found by Bartolomeo Cristofori, an instrument maker employed by the powerful Medici family in Florence, Italy. Around the year 1700, he built an instrument in which the strings were struck by small hammers covered in leather. The key feature of his design was a mechanism that allowed each hammer to strike the string and immediately fall back, so that the string could continue to vibrate. Because the force of the hammer depended on how hard the key was pressed, the player could now control the volume. Cristofori called his instrument the gravicembalo col piano e forte, meaning 'harpsichord with soft and loud', and it is from this name that the word piano comes.

Cristofori's invention attracted little attention at first. Only three of his pianos survive today, in museums in New York, Rome and Leipzig. It was in Germany, rather than Italy, that the instrument began to develop. The organ builder Gottfried Silbermann made pianos based on Cristofori's design and showed one to Johann Sebastian Bach in the 1730s. According to one account, Bach criticised the instrument's heavy touch and weak upper notes, but he later approved of an improved version.

By the late eighteenth century, the piano had become fashionable throughout Europe, and composers such as Mozart and Haydn wrote much of their keyboard music for it. Instruments of this period, now often called fortepianos, were much lighter than modern pianos, with wooden frames and thinner strings. Their sound was softer and faded more quickly. As composers demanded greater power and range, piano makers responded by adding more keys and using thicker strings under greater tension. Beethoven, in particular, was known for pushing the instruments of his time to their limits, and he is said to have broken strings when he played.

The greater tension of the strings created a problem: wooden frames could not withstand it and tended to bend or crack. The answer was iron. In 1825, the American maker Alpheus Babcock patented a frame cast in a single piece of iron, which allowed strings to be tightened much more. Later in the century, the firm founded in New York in 1853 by the German immigrant Henry Steinway combined an iron frame with an arrangement in which the bass strings crossed over the others, producing a richer and more powerful sound. By the 1880s, the piano had taken essentially its modern form, with eighty-eight keys covering more than seven octaves.

The nineteenth century also saw the piano move from the homes of the wealthy to those of the middle classes. Industrial production made instruments cheaper, and they could often be bought in instalments. Owning a piano became a symbol of respectability, and learning to play was considered an important accomplishment, especially for young women. Before the invention of the gramophone and the radio, the piano was the main way in which most people heard music at home, and publishers sold enormous quantities of sheet music, including piano arrangements of popular songs and operas.

In the twentieth century, the piano faced competition from recorded music and, later, from electronic keyboards, which are lighter, cheaper and can be played with headphones. Sales of traditional pianos have fallen in many countries. In China, however, where tens of millions of children are estimated to be learning the instrument, demand has grown enormously, and China is now the world's largest producer of pianos. More than three hundred years after Cristofori, his invention remains at the heart of musical life.

readingPassages.title: Why does music give us chills?
paragraphs: Many people have had the experience: a piece of music reaches a particular moment, and suddenly a shiver runs down the spine, the skin breaks out in goosebumps and the hairs on the arms stand on end. Psychologists call this response 'frisson', from a French word meaning a shiver or thrill. For a long time it was regarded as too personal and unpredictable to be studied scientifically. Today, however, it is the subject of a growing body of research, which is shedding light not only on music but on how the brain experiences pleasure.

Frisson is surprisingly common, but not universal. Surveys suggest that somewhere between half and two-thirds of people experience it at least occasionally when listening to music, although estimates vary considerably depending on how the question is asked. For some people, it happens frequently; others report never having felt it at all. The same piece of music may produce chills in one listener and leave another completely unmoved, and even the same listener may react differently on different occasions.

Researchers have identified several musical features that are particularly likely to produce chills. These include a sudden change in volume, such as a quiet passage followed by a loud one, the entrance of a new instrument or voice, and unexpected harmonies. What these features have in common is that they involve something surprising or that breaks a pattern the listener has come to expect. According to one theory, the brain is constantly predicting what will happen next in a piece of music, and chills occur when those predictions are violated in a way that is surprising but ultimately pleasurable.

The first brain-imaging study of musical chills was carried out in 2001 by Anne Blood and Robert Zatorre at McGill University in Montreal. They asked participants to bring in pieces of music that reliably gave them chills, and scanned their brains while they listened. They found that the experience was associated with activity in regions of the brain that are involved in reward and motivation, the same areas that respond to food, sex and certain drugs. This was a striking finding, because music, unlike food, has no obvious value for survival.

A later study by Valorie Salimpoor, also working with Zatorre, went further. Using a technique that can detect the release of chemicals in the brain, the researchers showed in 2011 that dopamine, a chemical associated with pleasure and reward, was released when listeners experienced the peak emotional moments of a piece. More surprisingly, dopamine was also released in a different area in the seconds before those moments, while listeners were anticipating them. In other words, part of the pleasure of music seems to come from the expectation of what is about to happen.

Why do some people experience chills more than others? Personality appears to play a role. Several studies have found that people who score highly on a personality trait known as openness to experience, which includes imagination, curiosity and a love of art and beauty, are more likely to report chills. There may also be differences in brain structure. A study by Matthew Sachs and colleagues at Harvard University in 2016, though based on only twenty participants, found that people who experienced chills had stronger connections between the areas of the brain that process sound and those that process emotion.

Context and memory matter too. Music that is associated with important events in a person's life, such as a wedding or the loss of a loved one, is especially likely to produce strong emotional responses. Some researchers have also noted that sad music produces chills particularly often. One explanation is that the experience resembles the physical response to separation or loss, combined with a sense of comfort and connection, which may explain why people seek out sad music even though it makes them feel sad.

The study of musical chills has practical as well as theoretical value. Because music can activate the brain's reward system so powerfully, researchers are investigating whether it could be used to help people with depression, a condition in which the ability to feel pleasure is often reduced. Others are interested in how music can motivate people during exercise or rehabilitation. Above all, the research shows that our response to music, far from being trivial, is rooted in some of the most fundamental systems of the human brain.

readingPassages.title: Should the arts be paid for by the state?
paragraphs: In most European countries, governments spend significant sums of public money on the arts. Opera houses, orchestras, theatres, museums and galleries receive grants that allow them to keep ticket prices lower than they would otherwise be, to commission new work and to take risks that commercial organisations might avoid. In the United States, by contrast, direct government funding is relatively small, and the arts depend much more on private donations, which are encouraged by tax relief. Whether, and how much, taxpayers should support the arts is a question that provokes strong opinions on all sides.

The tradition of public support for the arts has deep roots. For centuries, artists and musicians depended on wealthy patrons, such as kings, aristocrats and the Church. Haydn spent most of his career as a court musician employed by the Esterházy family in Hungary, and much of the greatest art of the Italian Renaissance was paid for by bankers and popes. As the power of these patrons declined, governments gradually took on part of their role. In Britain, the Arts Council was established in 1946, inspired partly by the economist John Maynard Keynes, who believed that the arts should be available to all and not only to the wealthy.

Supporters of public funding make several arguments. The first is economic. The cultural sector employs large numbers of people and attracts tourists, who spend money in hotels, restaurants and shops. Cities such as Bilbao in Spain, whose economy was transformed after the opening of the Guggenheim Museum in 1997, are often cited as evidence that investment in culture can bring wider benefits. The second argument concerns access. Without subsidies, it is claimed, tickets for opera, ballet or classical concerts would be so expensive that only the rich could attend.

A third argument is that the arts have value that cannot be measured in money. They help societies understand themselves, preserve cultural heritage for future generations and give people experiences of beauty and meaning. Some research also suggests that taking part in arts activities can improve health and well-being, particularly among older people and those who are socially isolated. In my view, this is ultimately the strongest argument, since it does not depend on the arts paying for themselves.

Critics, however, raise important objections. One is that public funding often benefits those who are already advantaged. Surveys in several countries have found that audiences for subsidised art forms such as opera and classical music are, on average, wealthier and more highly educated than the population as a whole. If this is the case, then taxes paid by people who never attend are effectively being used to subsidise the leisure activities of the better off. Supporters reply that the solution is to widen access, not to cut funding.

Another objection concerns who decides what is worth funding. When government bodies distribute grants, they inevitably make judgements about which kinds of art are valuable. Critics argue that this can favour established institutions and traditional forms over popular culture, or that it can lead to political interference. Others worry that dependence on public money can make arts organisations less responsive to audiences, since their income does not depend on selling tickets.

The economic arguments, too, have been questioned. Some economists point out that claims about the economic benefits of the arts are often based on studies commissioned by arts organisations themselves, and that money spent on culture might produce similar or greater benefits if it were spent on something else. The 'Bilbao effect', they note, has proved difficult to repeat; several cities that built expensive new museums in the hope of attracting tourists have been disappointed.

In practice, most countries now combine public and private funding, and the debate is less about whether the state should support the arts than about how much, and on what terms. Many governments now require funded organisations to demonstrate that they are reaching a wider and more diverse audience, through education programmes, cheaper tickets for young people and performances in schools, hospitals and community venues, and some publish detailed information about who attends their events. Whether such measures can answer the criticism that subsidised culture serves mainly a privileged minority remains to be seen.
